newsitem.title: USA: U.S. offers help in confirming drug lord's death.
newsitem.headline: U.S. offers help in confirming drug lord's death.

text.p: The United States has offered to perform post-mortem tests on the alleged body of drug kingpin Amado Carrillo Fuentes to dispel any doubts about the identity of the corpse, a senior U.S. drug agent said on Monday.
So far, Mexican officials have not accepted the U.S. offer, said Ernest Howard, special agent in charge of the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) office in Texas.

"Our government would love to have a chance to go down and do a full forensic (examination) on the body. Whether that's going to happen or not, I don't know. It has been offered ... as far as I know it has not been accepted," Howard told Reuters.

Carrillo Fuentes reportedly died on Friday in a Mexico City hospital from complications following plastic surgery. DEA chief Thomas Constantine confirmed the death in a statement from Washington, but there are lingering doubts.
"Right now we're being told by Mexican authorities it is Amado. They're in the process of doing DNA testing so we have to go along with the idea that it was," Howard said.

Adding to the mystery of the drug lord's alleged demise was its occurrence on the eve of Mexico's historic elections on Sunday. "We thought it was kind of unusual this all happened on Friday and Saturday," Howard said.

But, he said, there was no doubt Carrillo Fuentes had been in the process of changing his appearance through plastic surgery, liposuction and dieting in preparation for making the leap into a new life.

Howard said Carrillo Fuentes, also known as "The Lord of the Skies" for his tactic of flying in shipments of Colombian cocaine, was worried that Mexico was going to allow his extradition to the United States for trial on drug charges.
He recently had gone to Russia, Australia, South America and elsewhere scouting for a safe haven away from U.S. drug agents who have pursued him for years, Howard said.

Carrillo Fuentes was considered Mexico's top cocaine trafficker and as such was the number one target for U.S. agents. He faced U.S. drug indictments in Miami and Dallas and criminal investigations targeting him and were continuing.

Howard said the death of Carrillo Fuentes would not affect the investigations, including the probe into possible links between drug lords and Raul Salinas, the jailed brother of former Mexican President Carlos Salinas de Gortari.
